title: Tunneling-induced translation of intact $π$-radical clusters on Au(111)
authors: Jacob D. Teeter, Kateryna Averchenko, Maximilian Eliasch, Stefan Müllegger
abstract: The scanning tunneling microscope (STM) is a powerful tool for investigating and manipulating molecules on surfaces. We demonstrate with a low-temperature STM operated at 6.2 K the controlled manipulation of ternary clusters of persistent molecular $π$ radicals as a whole. The ternary clusters $-$ each self-assembled from three $α,γ$-bisdiphenylene-$β$-phenylallyl (BDPA) molecules on Au(111) $-$ maintain their natural cluster structure throughout tip-induced translation and rotation relative to the surface. Sustained and repeated dragging of radical clusters is shown to facilitate the construction of artificial assemblies of several clusters. Our results provide new opportunities for the creation and investigation of radical-based spin assemblies on surfaces.
summary: Using low-temperature STM, the researchers demonstrated the ability to precisely manipulate intact clusters of $\pi$-radical molecules adsorbed on Au(111). By applying voltage pulses, they induced sustained translation and rotation, proving that the entire cluster moves coherently. This work opens new avenues for building artificial quantum assemblies using molecular radicals.
main_problem: The research aims to demonstrate controlled, whole-cluster manipulation of intact $\pi$-radical clusters adsorbed on a metal surface.
main_result: The authors successfully achieved sustained and repeated dragging of ternary radical clusters, enabling the construction of artificial assemblies of these molecular units.
method: Manipulation was performed using low-temperature Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) by applying controlled voltage pulses to induce translational motion.
model_or_system: The system involves ternary clusters formed from $\alpha,\gamma$-bisdiphenylene-$ eta$-phenylallyl (BDPA) molecules adsorbed on the Au(111) surface. The experiment is conducted at 6.2 K using STM.
key_observables: Discrete jumps in tunnel current $I(t)$ corresponding to cluster translation or rotation, and the ability to construct artificial assemblies.
important_parameters: Low temperature (6.2 K); voltage pulses ($\ge |V| \ge 2 	ext{ V}$); sustained dragging speeds ($\le 1.5 	ext{ nm/s}$).
main_assumptions: The attractive force driving translation is attributed to an electric dipole moment induced by the strong, inhomogeneous electric field near the STM tip.
figures_summary: Figures show time-dependent current jumps during manipulation (Fig. 2), cluster rotation/translation (Fig. 3), and sequences demonstrating controlled dragging across the surface (Fig. 5).
paper_structure: The paper details using low-temperature STM to observe that entire radical clusters move as single units when subjected to voltage pulses, providing evidence for controllable assembly building.
why_interesting: This work provides an experimental platform for studying controlled quantum dynamics and interactions of molecular assemblies on surfaces, relevant to understanding engineered quantum materials or artificial lattices.
